ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Bergische Universität Wuppertal (ref. no.
SK/AE 240113) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Participants were adolescents and young adults aged 14-21 residing in Germany who had migrated themselves or had at least one parent who had migrated; inclusion criteria were confirmed by telephone.
Most were still in school (69.68%), 20.32% were enrolled at university, and most described their financial situation as average (41.61%) or good (43.23%).
Consistent with a dimensional, transdiagnostic framework, participants were recruited to span a broad range of symptom expression, including adolescents engaged and not engaged in clinical services.
Participants completed an in-person debriefing session, with compensation following a tiered structure based on compliance (maximum €125) 1.

Participants completed on average 25.98 entries (SD = 4.54, Mdn = 28; 89.59% of possible, range = 13.79-100%); 95.48% of participants completed at least 50% and 82.26% at least 80% of surveys, meeting or exceeding typical compliance in adolescent daily-diary research on discrimination (60%-90%; Wang et al., 2026).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Power Considerations. Because the dataset was designed as a resource for multiple research questions, the sample size target prioritized estimation precision over conventional statistical power. Following Schönbrodt and Perugini (2013), we targeted a minimum of N = 250 for stable correlation estimates (±.10 precision) and oversampled to N = 300 ethnoracially minoritized youth to account for attrition (the larger data collection, targeting N = 450, also included participants without migration history).

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Daily Stress and Psychopathology Over One Month in Ethnoracially Minoritized Youth
table.research_questions:
Research Questions and Hypotheses

RQ1: To what extent can a modified broad symptom inventory consistently capture within-person fluctuations across diverse domains of psychopathology in youths’ daily lives (i.e. examination of (factorial) validity, reliability, multilevel variance decomposition, stability and context-sensitivity).

RQs 1.1–1.3 pertain to the first goal of the study—evaluating the psychometric properties and construct validity of the daily symptom short form—and are therefore designated as exploratory. While our approach is guided by prior theoretical frameworks and empirical findings (e.g., Wright et al., 2025), psychometric evaluations—such as assessing factor structure, reliability, and multilevel variance decomposition—are typically not framed as formal hypothesis tests. Instead of confirming a specific directional prediction, these analyses aim to assess the suitability and robustness of the measurement model in a new population and context (i.e., ethnoracially minoritized youth in a daily diary format). In contrast, the formal hypotheses (H1–H3) focus on theoretically derived, directional predictions about (dynamic) associations between daily experiences and symptoms. This distinction ensures conceptual clarity and aligns our analytic strategy with best practices in psychometric and developmental research.

RQ.1.1.: What is the hierarchical structure of psychopathology dimensions both at the within-person (daily variability) and between-person (individual differences) levels?

Based on Wright et al. (2025), we expect a multidimensional within-person structure of psychopathology to emerge in daily life, with key domains—such as Internalizing, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, Anankastia, and Psychoticism—showing meaningful variability over time within individuals. 
We will assess the proportion of variance attributable to within-person fluctuations versus between-person differences at the domain level and examine whether these domains covary in theoretically consistent ways. This approach rests on the assumption that the structure of symptom covariation at the within-person level parallels that observed between individuals—an idea that has been the subject of ongoing debate. Molenaar (2004) questioned this parallelism, highlighting the potential heterogeneity of within-person structures and the risk of overlooking idiographic variation in group-level models. However, others have reported empirical evidence for structural similarities across levels when focusing on average within-person patterns (Borkenau & Ostendorf, 1998; Ringwald et al., 2022, Wright et al., 2025; Zimmermann et al., 2019), though some note that average within-person structures may be less clearly defined in specific domains. While our study cannot settle this debate, it contributes to the discussion by jointly modeling both levels of variance in an adolescent sample. Following Wright et al. (2025), we focus on average within-person patterns, hypothesizing that the same domains of psychopathology that covary between individuals also covary within individuals on a day-to-day basis, suggesting a shared latent structure.
RQ.1.2.: To what extent do individuals’ average daily levels of psychopathology align with established baseline assessments (e.g., self-report inventories)?
We anticipate that daily assessments of psychopathology will align well with established baseline measures (e.g., YSR, PID-5), supporting the validity of the daily measure.

RQ1.3: To what extent do daily measures of psychopathology correlate with daily ratings of affect, well-being, and emotion regulation?
This question explores whether within-person (day-level) fluctuations in psychopathology measures show theoretically plausible patterns of covariation with affective and behavioral indicators—such as higher negative affect and lower perceived emotion regulation efficacy on days with elevated symptom levels. While not hypothesized formally, such associations would support the construct validity of the daily psychopathology measures.
RQ.2.: How do daily experiences of discrimination and general stressors influence within-person fluctuations in psychopathology?

To contextualize and better understand daily within-person variability in psychopathology, we will examine patterns of symptom reactivity and carryover—specifically, how youths’ reported symptoms co-vary with daily experiences of stress. This approach allows us to explore not only whether symptoms fluctuate from day to day, but how these fluctuations may relate to specific situational factors (e.g., experiences of racial discrimination, more general daily stressors). By modeling these dynamic person-by-context associations, we aim to gain insight into potential processes that may coincide with the intensification or persistence of symptoms in youths’ everyday lives, without assuming causal effects.


Concurrent Associations (reactivity)
H.1.1: On days when youth report experiences of (both directly or vicariously experienced) discrimination (dichotomous variable), they will report elevated levels of psychopathology relative to days without experiences of discrimination.
H.1.2: On days when youth report more severe experiences of (both directly or vicariously experienced) discrimination (continuous variable of severity), they will report elevated levels of psychopathology relative to days with less severe experiences of discrimination.
H.1.3: On days when youth report higher levels of (general) stress, they will  report elevated levels of psychopathology relative to days with lower levels of (general) stress.

Lagged Associations (temporal carryover effects)
H.2.1: Discrimination experiences (direct or vicarious; dichotomous) reported on day t will be positively associated with psychopathology on day t+1, after adjusting for psychopathology on day t (autoregressive effect).
H.2.2: The severity of discrimination experiences (direct or vicarious; continuous) reported on day t will positively predict psychopathology on day t+1, after adjusting for psychopathology on day t (autoregressive effect).
H.2.3: General stress reported on day t will be positively associated with psychopathology on day t+1, after adjusting for psychopathology on day t (autoregressive effect).
Between-Person Associations
RQ.3.: To what extent do individuals’ average daily levels of psychopathology align with aggregated levels of (both directly and vicariously experienced) discrimination and general stress? We expect that individuals who report higher average levels of daily discrimination also tend to report more severe mental health symptoms (as a theoretically grounded test of construct validity). 
H.3.: Youth who, on average, report more frequent experiences of discrimination or general stress are also expected to report higher levels of psychopathology.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: The full protocol is described in detail elsewhere: https://osf.io/dqv8f/. Participants are recruited through a combination of community networks, online platforms, and flyers distributed in the city center. In total, 104 organizations and institutions are contacted, resulting in 55 successful collaborations. Recruitment targets a variety of community-based settings, with schools representing the largest share (40 contacts), followed by local clubs and associations (17 contacts). Additional outreach includes cultural venues (e.g., cinemas, event spaces), youth centers, cafés/bars/clubs, municipal institutions, and healthcare services, though these are contacted less frequently (2–9 instances each). At the time of reporting, several contacts—particularly with schools and clubs—remain pending, suggesting that recruitment through these channels may continue. Eligibility requires participants to attend both an introductory (baseline) and closing session in person, which restricts participation to those living near the study site. To minimize self-selection bias, the study is broadly advertised as focusing on youths' everyday experiences, without explicitly referencing discrimination or migration history.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: At the time of preregistration, some data were already available, as preregistration occurred during the ongoing data collection period. However, with the exception of participant-level compliance rates and mean compliance within a subset of the sample, no data were accessed or subjected to analysis prior to preregistration. Compliance analyses were conducted solely for the purpose of determining engagement-contingent compensation and were carried out by a research assistant who remained blind to the study’s hypotheses and analytic plan.

table.sample_size:
For our most conservative analyses—particularly between-person associations in our hierarchical data structure (i.e., days nested within persons)—we targeted a minimum sample size of N = 250. Anticipating some dropout or partial engagement with the ESM protocol following baseline, we oversampled, aiming for a final sample of N = 300.
(see "sample size rationale" for full overview)
table.sample_size_rationale: Our dataset was designed as a flexible resource for investigating a broad range of research questions, with an emphasis on estimating a variety of effect sizes rather than testing specific hypotheses. We anticipated that most analyses would use covariance or correlation-based methods, such as structural equation modeling and multilevel modeling. Accordingly, our primary goal in determining sample size was to obtain stable effect estimates, rather than to ensure statistical power for detecting specific effects. We also aimed to detect small effects, consistent with average effect sizes reported in the affect-regulation literature. Prior research indicates that correlation estimates stabilize around ±.10 with a probability of .80 when sample sizes approach N = 250 (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013). Therefore, for our most conservative analyses—particularly between-person associations in our hierarchical data structure (i.e., days nested within persons)—we targeted a minimum sample size of N = 250. Anticipating some dropout or partial engagement with the ESM protocol following baseline, we oversampled, aiming for a final sample of N = 300.

1.	For all analyses, each of the PID-5 domains—Negative Affectivity, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism—will be summarized using their mean values and analyzed both individually and as a composite total score. 


2.	From the retained pool of 90 YSR items, we will compute subscale scores based on the DSM-oriented scales as defined in the YSR manual and validated in the German adaptation (Döpfner et al., 2014). Specifically, we will focus on four core dimensions that align with our study's transdiagnostic framework and that map onto constructs assessed in the daily diary: Depression, Anxiety, Disinhibition (rule-breaking + aggressive behavior), and Inattention/Hyperactivity. Each DSM-oriented subscale will be computed by summing the relevant items (coded 0 = “not true,” 1 = “somewhat or sometimes true,” 2 = “very true or often true”), yielding a total raw score per subscale. Item-to-scale assignments will follow the structure specified in the YSR/11-18R scoring guidelines (Döpfner et al., 2014). Any missing values will be handled via person-mean imputation if no more than 20% of items on a given scale are missing; otherwise, the subscale will be set to missing for that participant. If needed for sensitivity analyses or dimensional modeling, we will also compute broader Internalizing and Externalizing summary scores by combining the relevant syndrome scales in line with Achenbach system conventions—specifically: (1) Internalizing = Anxiety/Depression + Withdrawn/Depressed + Somatic Complaints; (2) Externalizing = Rule-Breaking Behavior + Aggressive Behavior. However, primary analyses will focus on the DSM-oriented subscales due to their closer conceptual alignment with daily-assessed symptoms.


3.	Additionally, a total daily negative affect and a total daily positive affect score, calculated as the mean of the respective positively and negatively valenced items, will be used.


4.	To assess participants’ daily exposure to stress, we included a checklist of 14 common adolescent stressors (e.g., conflict with friends, negative feedback, worry about climate change), plus an open-response option (“Something else, namely…”). Each day, participants were first asked whether they had experienced anything stressful and, if applicable, to select the most stressful experience from the provided list. For the purpose of analyzing general daily stress, we will create a binary variable indicating whether any stressor was reported (1) or no stressor was reported (0) on a given day. This aggregated variable will serve as a marker of overall daily stress exposure, allowing us to examine associations between general stress and other variables such as daily psychopathology, affect, or coping. This approach balances analytic tractability with ecological validity, while more specific analyses can still draw on the type or content of reported stressors when needed.


5.	To capture the subjective impact of discriminatory experiences, participants were asked: “How did the situation feel?”, rated on an 11-point bipolar scale ranging from –5 = “very bad” to +5 = “very good”. This item was presented for both direct and vicarious discrimination events, as well as general social interactions. Importantly, this scale deviates from conventional unipolar severity measures (which typically assess impact from low to high). Instead, it reflects emotional valence, capturing both negatively and positively experienced events. While the scale was labeled "Severity", it more accurately indexes the subjective emotional impact of the reported event. On days without reported discrimination, participants were still prompted to rate an interaction, resulting in scores around 0 — which we interpret as reflecting neutral or no emotional impact. In practice, values below zero are expected to predominate on days when discrimination is reported, aligning with the construct’s theoretical framing. To maintain conceptual clarity in analyses, we will retain the full –5 to +5 range but provide a clear explanation that the term “severity” in this context refers to the negatively valenced end of the emotional impact spectrum. This approach avoids discarding meaningful variability in subjective experience while acknowledging the deviation from standard severity metrics.
table.statistical_tests:
Psychometric Evaluation
To address RQ 1.1, we will primarily use multilevel exploratory factor analysis (ML-EFA) to examine the factor structure of the daily psychopathology facet scales, expecting a higher-order multilevel factor structure of daily psychopathology scales. This approach is based on prior evidence supporting the structure of the 15-item short form (Wright et al., 2025) which showed good model fit (note that we included three additional items to capture Psychoticism-related variance). Based on Wright et al. (2025), we expect a six-factor solution to emerge (on both levels), representing all conceptually outlined domains: Internalizing, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, Anankastia, (and a possible additional factor reflecting) Psychoticism (-related variance). 
Internal consistency of daily facet scales will be assessed using Omega coefficients (ω) at both levels.  Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICCs) will be computed at the domain level to quantify the proportion of variance attributable to each level.
To address RQ 1.2 and RQ 1.3 we will use Multilevel Modeling (MLM) to examine associations between daily psychopathology and both baseline and momentary measures. Repeatedly sampling psychopathology will result in a hierarchical data structure: daily psychopathology assessments (within-person level) will be nested within individuals (between-person level). At the between-person level, we will assess convergent validity by modeling correlations between participants’ average daily psychopathology scores and established baseline assessments (e.g., YSR, PID-5). At the within-person level, we will examine day-to-day associations between fluctuations in psychopathology dimensions and daily affective and behavioral variables (e.g., affect, emotion regulation efficacy, well-being). We will test these bivariate associations (RQ 1.2 vs. RQ 1.3) in separate models. 

Tests of Preregistered Hypotheses
We will test hypothesized within-person effects of daily stressors, including perceived discrimination and (more general daily) stress, using Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM; McNeish et al., 2021). These analyses will address dynamic within-person effects (e.g., whether same-day or next-day fluctuations in stress predict increases in psychopathology; H1 and H2) and between-person effects (e.g., whether individuals reporting higher average levels of discrimination show higher overall psychopathology across the study period; H3).
DSEM also allows for the estimation of random slopes, which capture individual differences in the strength of within-person associations among daily variables, allowing to model patterns of reactivity. These random slopes can be conceptualized as between-person variables that reflect the extent to which two constructs are associated with each other over time within an individual. In addition, DSEM models include autoregressive effects, capturing the extent to which psychopathology levels on a given day are predicted by levels on the previous day, thus providing insight into symptom carryover and inertia. Taken together, this approach allows us to examine whether daily deviations from a participant’s typical levels of general stressors (e.g., discrimination, interpersonal conflict) are associated with corresponding deviations in psychopathology. Figure 2 provides a schematic overview of the estimated models.
In the case of dichotomous variables (e.g., daily discrimination experiences, stress), DSEM assumes an underlying normally distributed latent response variable. The observed binary outcome (e.g., occurrence vs. non-occurrence of discrimination) reflects whether this latent propensity exceeds a certain threshold (McNeish, Somers, & Savord, 2024). Thus, we do not model discrimination as a direct binary outcome, but rather the latent process underlying the binary response. Accordingly, our within-person interpretations will follow this logic — for example: “On days when youth show a higher latent propensity to experience (both direct and vicarious) discrimination, relative to days with lower latent propensity…”.
Concurrent Associations (H.1) and H.3. In six separate multilevel models (separating directly and vicariously experienced discrimination), we will test concurrent within-person associations between daily experiences and symptoms of psychopathology. Specifically, daily ratings of psychopathology will be regressed on same-day ratings of: directly or vicariously experienced discrimination (H.1.1; see further specifications via “exploratory analyses”), perceived severity of these discrimination experiences (i.e., the emotional impact; H.1.2), and general daily stress intensity (H.1.3). These hypotheses refer to the expected average strength of the within-person association between daily stressor exposure and symptom levels across individuals. While random slopes are included in the model to allow for individual variation, the hypotheses test whether the mean of these slopes differs from zero, rather than focusing on their variance..
At the between-person level, we will also examine whether person-level averages of stressor exposure are associated with person-level averages of psychopathology (H.3). 
Lagged Associations (H.2.1–H.2.3). To examine temporal carryover effects, we will use fully cross-lagged models (see McNeish & Hamaker, 2019). Specifically, we will test whether stressor experiences reported on day t (e.g., discrimination, general stress) predict levels of psychopathology on day t + 1, while controlling for psychopathology on day t (i.e., accounting for autoregressive effects). These models allow us to assess the temporal precedence of stressor effects and examine whether prior-day experiences contribute to next-day symptomatology.  Following convention in standard cross-lagged panel modeling, we do not include same-day (i.e., contemporaneous) paths between stressor exposure and psychopathology in these models. Instead, same-day associations in these models are captured via residual covariances between the two constructs at each time point. This approach is widely used, yields stable estimates, and allows for intuitive interpretation of lagged effects without overcomplicating the model structure (see also Muthén & Asparouhov, 2024). 
As a robustness check, we will estimate a residual DSEM model in which the autoregressive effects are specified on the residuals after removing the linear trend (McNeish & Hamaker, 2020). While this approach is theoretically recommended for isolating temporal dynamics, it is known to exhibit convergence issues and will therefore be treated as an exploratory extension.
All ML-EFA, and MLM models will be estimated using Maximum Likelihood estimation with scaled fit statistics and robust standard errors in Mplus (version 8.11; Muthén & Muthén, 2024; ESTIMATOR = MLR). DSEM models will be estimated using Bayesian parameter estimation (ESTIMATOR = BAYES). To promote stable estimation of DSEM models, BITERATIONS will initially be set to 1000 and increased if trace plots suggest insufficient convergence.
table.inference_criteria: Significance for all model parameters will be based on 95% Credibility Intervals (CIs), with CIs that excluded zero being indicative of a parameter that differs significantly from zero.
table.missing_data_handling:
Missing data will be handled under the assumption that data are missing at random, meaning the probability of missingness is unrelated to the observed variables in the model. This allows us to retain all available information for parameter estimation without biasing results. In line with best practices and Mplus defaults, we use non-informative (diffuse) priors and a Bayesian estimation framework, which—particularly with large samples—yields results comparable to Full Information Maximum Likelihood (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010). DSEM further accommodates missingness at the within-person level using a Kalman filter approach (Hamaker & Grasman, 2012; Kim & Nelson, 1999). The Kalman filter makes time-point-specific predictions based on lagged predictors, and updates these predictions when observations are available. If a data point is missing, the filter continues with its prior prediction, ensuring that no data points are discarded. This method enables robust estimation even when a substantial proportion of occasions are incomplete. Importantly, DSEM in Mplus does not require the dataset to have equally spaced observations. By specifying the time since the first measurement (using the TINTERVAL command), the model adjusts for varying intervals between observations automatically (Asparouhov et al., 2018). 
In addition to these model-based strategies, selected stressor-specific variables—including stress intensity and discrimination severity—will be handled through value replacement with zero in cases where a stressor was not reported on a given day. This coding reflects the conceptual assumption that a missing severity rating in the absence of a reported stressor indicates a value of zero, i.e., no subjective intensity or impact. This approach preserves the temporal structure of the data while maintaining interpretability and model parsimony, particularly in models evaluating stressor-specific reactivity.
table.exploratory_analyses:
In addition to the confirmatory hypotheses outlined above, we will conduct a series of exploratory analyses to better understand how the nature, context, and perceived meaning of daily stressors—particularly discrimination—shape adolescents’ psychopathological responses. These analyses are intended to generate new hypotheses and inform future confirmatory work.

1. Stressor-Specific Reactivity. We aim to examine whether certain types of daily stressors—captured in our “stress event” variables—moderate the within-person association between stressor exposure and daily fluctuations in psychopathology. For discrimination experiences, we will test the following dimensions as potential moderators: (1) frequency of unfair treatment (e.g., once, more than once, open-ended response), (2) context/location of the unfair experience (e.g., public vs. private, online vs. offline), (3) relationship to the perpetrator (e.g., stranger, peer/friend, teacher, parent/family member, authority figure), (4) attribution to prejudice, rated on a scale from 0 (“does not apply at all”) to 10 (“fully applies”).  These analyses aim to clarify which forms of discrimination are most psychologically impactful and how specific event characteristics shape adolescents’ daily symptom responses.

2. Discrimination Composite Variable. In tests of hypotheses H.1.1/H.2.1 and H.2.1/H.2.2, direct and vicarious experiences of discrimination will be further combined into a single composite variable. This decision is based on the expectedly relatively low frequency of individual categories. 

3. Symptom-Specific Reactivity Patterns. We will also explore whether within-person reactivity to stressors varies across dimensions of psychopathology. We will examine whether certain domains (e.g., internalizing symptoms such as depression and anxiety) show stronger day-to-day covariation with stressors than others (e.g., detachment, anankastia). This may offer insight into domain-specific vulnerability patterns and help identify targets for intervention.

4. Incremental Effects of Daily Experiences of Discrimination. We will conduct additional analyses to test whether (the severity of) daily discrimination events contribute(s) uniquely to same-day and next-day psychopathology beyond the effects of other stressors. These analyses allow to assess the incremental impact of discrimination severity on adolescents’ psychological functioning and the potential for delayed symptom responses. Amending H.1.4, we will examine whether higher discrimination severity (direct or vicarious), as rated by participants, predicts same-day increases in psychopathology, after adjusting for the effect of same-day general stress. This analysis tests whether the psychological effects of discrimination are distinct from those of general daily stressors, and whether severity ratings add explanatory value above simple occurrence. Amending H.2.4, we will investigate whether discrimination severity on a given day predicts next-day psychopathology, controlling for general stress on day t (incremental effect) and psychopathology on day t (autoregressive effect).

RQ1: To what extent can a modified broad symptom inventory consistently capture within-person fluctuations across diverse domains of psychopathology in youths’ daily lives (i.e. examination of (factorial) validity, reliability, multilevel variance decomposition, stability and context-sensitivity).

RQs 1.1–1.3 pertain to the first goal of the study—evaluating the psychometric properties and construct validity of the daily symptom short form—and are therefore designated as exploratory. While our approach is guided by prior theoretical frameworks and empirical findings (e.g., Wright et al., 2025), psychometric evaluations—such as assessing factor structure, reliability, and multilevel variance decomposition—are typically not framed as formal hypothesis tests. Instead of confirming a specific directional prediction, these analyses aim to assess the suitability and robustness of the measurement model in a new population and context (i.e., ethnoracially minoritized youth in a daily diary format). In contrast, the formal hypotheses (H1–H3) focus on theoretically derived, directional predictions about (dynamic) associations between daily experiences and symptoms. This distinction ensures conceptual clarity and aligns our analytic strategy with best practices in psychometric and developmental research.

RQ.1.1.: What is the hierarchical structure of psychopathology dimensions both at the within-person (daily variability) and between-person (individual differences) levels?

Based on Wright et al. (2025), we expect a multidimensional within-person structure of psychopathology to emerge in daily life, with key domains—such as Internalizing, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, Anankastia, and Psychoticism—showing meaningful variability over time within individuals.
We will assess the proportion of variance attributable to within-person fluctuations versus between-person differences at the domain level and examine whether these domains covary in theoretically consistent ways. This approach rests on the assumption that the structure of symptom covariation at the within-person level parallels that observed between individuals—an idea that has been the subject of ongoing debate. Molenaar (2004) questioned this parallelism, highlighting the potential heterogeneity of within-person structures and the risk of overlooking idiographic variation in group-level models. However, others have reported empirical evidence for structural similarities across levels when focusing on average within-person patterns (Borkenau & Ostendorf, 1998; Ringwald et al., 2022, Wright et al., 2025; Zimmermann et al., 2019), though some note that average within-person structures may be less clearly defined in specific domains. While our study cannot settle this debate, it contributes to the discussion by jointly modeling both levels of variance in an adolescent sample. Following Wright et al. (2025), we focus on average within-person patterns, hypothesizing that the same domains of psychopathology that covary between individuals also covary within individuals on a day-to-day basis, suggesting a shared latent structure.
RQ.1.2.: To what extent do individuals’ average daily levels of psychopathology align with established baseline assessments (e.g., self-report inventories)?
We anticipate that daily assessments of psychopathology will align well with established baseline measures (e.g., YSR, PID-5), supporting the validity of the daily measure.

RQ1.3: To what extent do daily measures of psychopathology correlate with daily ratings of affect, well-being, and emotion regulation?
This question explores whether within-person (day-level) fluctuations in psychopathology measures show theoretically plausible patterns of covariation with affective and behavioral indicators—such as higher negative affect and lower perceived emotion regulation efficacy on days with elevated symptom levels. While not hypothesized formally, such associations would support the construct validity of the daily psychopathology measures.
RQ.2.: How do daily experiences of discrimination and general stressors influence within-person fluctuations in psychopathology?

To contextualize and better understand daily within-person variability in psychopathology, we will examine patterns of symptom reactivity and carryover—specifically, how youths’ reported symptoms co-vary with daily experiences of stress. This approach allows us to explore not only whether symptoms fluctuate from day to day, but how these fluctuations may relate to specific situational factors (e.g., experiences of racial discrimination, more general daily stressors). By modeling these dynamic person-by-context associations, we aim to gain insight into potential processes that may coincide with the intensification or persistence of symptoms in youths’ everyday lives, without assuming causal effects.


Concurrent Associations (reactivity)
H.1.1: On days when youth report experiences of (both directly or vicariously experienced) discrimination (dichotomous variable), they will report elevated levels of psychopathology relative to days without experiences of discrimination.
H.1.2: On days when youth report more severe experiences of (both directly or vicariously experienced) discrimination (continuous variable of severity), they will report elevated levels of psychopathology relative to days with less severe experiences of discrimination.
H.1.3: On days when youth report higher levels of (general) stress, they will report elevated levels of psychopathology relative to days with lower levels of (general) stress.

Lagged Associations (temporal carryover effects)
H.2.1: Discrimination experiences (direct or vicarious; dichotomous) reported on day t will be positively associated with psychopathology on day t+1, after adjusting for psychopathology on day t (autoregressive effect).
H.2.2: The severity of discrimination experiences (direct or vicarious; continuous) reported on day t will positively predict psychopathology on day t+1, after adjusting for psychopathology on day t (autoregressive effect).
H.2.3: General stress reported on day t will be positively associated with psychopathology on day t+1, after adjusting for psychopathology on day t (autoregressive effect).
Between-Person Associations
RQ.3.: To what extent do individuals’ average daily levels of psychopathology align with aggregated levels of (both directly and vicariously experienced) discrimination and general stress? We expect that individuals who report higher average levels of daily discrimination also tend to report more severe mental health symptoms (as a theoretically grounded test of construct validity).

We will test hypothesized within-person effects of daily stressors, including perceived discrimination and (more general daily) stress, using Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM; McNeish et al., 2021). These analyses will address dynamic within-person effects (e.g., whether same-day or next-day fluctuations in stress predict increases in psychopathology; H1 and H2) and between-person effects (e.g., whether individuals reporting higher average levels of discrimination show higher overall psychopathology across the study period; H3).
DSEM also allows for the estimation of random slopes, which capture individual differences in the strength of within-person associations among daily variables, allowing to model patterns of reactivity. These random slopes can be conceptualized as between-person variables that reflect the extent to which two constructs are associated with each other over time within an individual. In addition, DSEM models include autoregressive effects, capturing the extent to which psychopathology levels on a given day are predicted by levels on the previous day, thus providing insight into symptom carryover and inertia. Taken together, this approach allows us to examine whether daily deviations from a participant’s typical levels of general stressors (e.g., discrimination, interpersonal conflict) are associated with corresponding deviations in psychopathology. Figure 2 provides a schematic overview of the estimated models.
In the case of dichotomous variables (e.g., daily discrimination experiences, stress), DSEM assumes an underlying normally distributed latent response variable. The observed binary outcome (e.g., occurrence vs. non-occurrence of discrimination) reflects whether this latent propensity exceeds a certain threshold (McNeish, Somers, & Savord, 2024). Thus, we do not model discrimination as a direct binary outcome, but rather the latent process underlying the binary response. Accordingly, our within-person interpretations will follow this logic — for example: “On days when youth show a higher latent propensity to experience (both direct and vicarious) discrimination, relative to days with lower latent propensity…”.
Concurrent Associations (H.1) and H.3. In six separate multilevel models (separating directly and vicariously experienced discrimination), we will test concurrent within-person associations between daily experiences and symptoms of psychopathology. Specifically, daily ratings of psychopathology will be regressed on same-day ratings of: directly or vicariously experienced discrimination (H.1.1; see further specifications via “exploratory analyses”), perceived severity of these discrimination experiences (i.e., the emotional impact; H.1.2), and general daily stress intensity (H.1.3). These hypotheses refer to the expected average strength of the within-person association between daily stressor exposure and symptom levels across individuals. While random slopes are included in the model to allow for individual variation, the hypotheses test whether the mean of these slopes differs from zero, rather than focusing on their variance..
At the between-person level, we will also examine whether person-level averages of stressor exposure are associated with person-level averages of psychopathology (H.3).
Lagged Associations (H.2.1–H.2.3). To examine temporal carryover effects, we will use fully cross-lagged models (see McNeish & Hamaker, 2019). Specifically, we will test whether stressor experiences reported on day t (e.g., discrimination, general stress) predict levels of psychopathology on day t + 1, while controlling for psychopathology on day t (i.e., accounting for autoregressive effects). These models allow us to assess the temporal precedence of stressor effects and examine whether prior-day experiences contribute to next-day symptomatology. Following convention in standard cross-lagged panel modeling, we do not include same-day (i.e., contemporaneous) paths between stressor exposure and psychopathology in these models. Instead, same-day associations in these models are captured via residual covariances between the two constructs at each time point. This approach is widely used, yields stable estimates, and allows for intuitive interpretation of lagged effects without overcomplicating the model structure (see also Muthén & Asparouhov, 2024).
As a robustness check, we will estimate a residual DSEM model in which the autoregressive effects are specified on the residuals after removing the linear trend (McNeish & Hamaker, 2020). While this approach is theoretically recommended for isolating temporal dynamics, it is known to exhibit convergence issues and will therefore be treated as an exploratory extension.
All ML-EFA, and MLM models will be estimated using Maximum Likelihood estimation with scaled fit statistics and robust standard errors in Mplus (version 8.11; Muthén & Muthén, 2024; ESTIMATOR = MLR). DSEM models will be estimated using Bayesian parameter estimation (ESTIMATOR = BAYES). To promote stable estimation of DSEM models, BITERATIONS will initially be set to 1000 and increased if trace plots suggest insufficient convergence.", "s. Indices", "Significance for all model parameters will be based on 95% Credibility Intervals (CIs), with CIs that excluded zero being indicative of a parameter that differs significantly from zero.", "Missing data will be handled under the assumption that data are missing at random, meaning the probability of missingness is unrelated to the observed variables in the model. This allows us to retain all available information for parameter estimation without biasing results. In line with best practices and Mplus defaults, we use non-informative (diffuse) priors and a Bayesian estimation framework, which—particularly with large samples—yields results comparable to Full Information Maximum Likelihood (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010). DSEM further accommodates missingness at the within-person level using a Kalman filter approach (Hamaker & Grasman, 2012; Kim & Nelson, 1999). The Kalman filter makes time-point-specific predictions based on lagged predictors, and updates these predictions when observations are available. If a data point is missing, the filter continues with its prior prediction, ensuring that no data points are discarded. This method enables robust estimation even when a substantial proportion of occasions are incomplete. Importantly, DSEM in Mplus does not require the dataset to have equally spaced observations. By specifying the time since the first measurement (using the TINTERVAL command), the model adjusts for varying intervals between observations automatically (Asparouhov et al., 2018).
In addition to these model-based strategies, selected stressor-specific variables—including stress intensity and discrimination severity—will be handled through value replacement with zero in cases where a stressor was not reported on a given day. This coding reflects the conceptual assumption that a missing severity rating in the absence of a reported stressor indicates a value of zero, i.e., no subjective intensity or impact. This approach preserves the temporal structure of the data while maintaining interpretability and model parsimony, particularly in models evaluating stressor-specific reactivity.", "In addition to the confirmatory hypotheses outlined above, we will conduct a series of exploratory analyses to better understand how the nature, context, and perceived meaning of daily stressors—particularly discrimination—shape adolescents’ psychopathological responses. These analyses are intended to generate new hypotheses and inform future confirmatory work.

1. Stressor-Specific Reactivity. We aim to examine whether certain types of daily stressors—captured in our “stress event” variables—moderate the within-person association between stressor exposure and daily fluctuations in psychopathology. For discrimination experiences, we will test the following dimensions as potential moderators: (1) frequency of unfair treatment (e.g., once, more than once, open-ended response), (2) context/location of the unfair experience (e.g., public vs. private, online vs. offline), (3) relationship to the perpetrator (e.g., stranger, peer/friend, teacher, parent/family member, authority figure), (4) attribution to prejudice, rated on a scale from 0 (“does not apply at all”) to 10 (“fully applies”). These analyses aim to clarify which forms of discrimination are most psychologically impactful and how specific event characteristics shape adolescents’ daily symptom responses.

2. Discrimination Composite Variable. In tests of hypotheses H.1.1/H.2.1 and H.2.1/H.2.2, direct and vicarious experiences of discrimination will be further combined into a single composite variable. This decision is based on the expectedly relatively low frequency of individual categories.

3. Symptom-Specific Reactivity Patterns. We will also explore whether within-person reactivity to stressors varies across dimensions of psychopathology. We will examine whether certain domains (e.g., internalizing symptoms such as depression and anxiety) show stronger day-to-day covariation with stressors than others (e.g., detachment, anankastia). This may offer insight into domain-specific vulnerability patterns and help identify targets for intervention.

4. Incremental Effects of Daily Experiences of Discrimination. We will conduct additional analyses to test whether (the severity of) daily discrimination events contribute(s) uniquely to same-day and next-day psychopathology beyond the effects of other stressors. These analyses allow to assess the incremental impact of discrimination severity on adolescents’ psychological functioning and the potential for delayed symptom responses. Amending H.1.4, we will examine whether higher discrimination severity (direct or vicarious), as rated by participants, predicts same-day increases in psychopathology, after adjusting for the effect of same-day general stress. This analysis tests whether the psychological effects of discrimination are distinct from those of general daily stressors, and whether severity ratings add explanatory value above simple occurrence. Amending H.2.4, we will investigate whether discrimination severity on a given day predicts next-day psychopathology, controlling for general stress on day t (incremental effect) and psychopathology on day t (autoregressive effect).", "For more detailed information, please see the PDF files uploaded in the folder titled \"Measuring Psychopathology in the Daily Lives of Ethnically Minoritized Youth (https://osf.io/dqv8f/).", "input")), row.names = c("template_name", "title", "id", "link", "date_created", "date_modified", "date_registered", "embargo_end_date", "ia_url", "research_questions", "study_type", "blinding", "study_design_overview", "existing_data", "existing_data_explanation", "data_collection_procedures", "sample_size", "sample_size_rationale", "manipulated_variables", "measured_variables", "indices", "statistical_tests", "transformations", "inference_criteria", "missing_data_handling", "exploratory_analyses", "additional_comments", "paper_id"), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of deviations from preregistrations, see: van den Akker O, Bakker M, van Assen M, Pennington C, Verweij L, Elsherif M, Claesen A, Gaillard S, Yeung S, Frankenberger J, Krautter K, Cockcroft J, Kreuer K, Evans T, Heppel F, Schoch S, Korbmacher M, Yamada Y, Albayrak-Aydemir N, Wicherts J (2024). “The potential of preregistration in psychology: Assessing preregistration producibility and preregistration-study consistency.” Psychological Methods. doi:10.1037/met0000687. report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .05", "ps > .05", "p < .05"
), Text = c("Daily Anankastia showed the strongest discriminant pattern overall-unrelated to PID-5 Negative Affectivity, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism (rs = .01-.08, all ps > .05)-though small significant correlations with PID-5 Antagonism (r = .23) and Detachment (r = .12) indicate the pattern was not entirely clean.", 
"Daily anankastia was essentially uncorrelated with every YSR scale (|r| ≤ .05, all ps > .05), consistent with the absence of Anankastia content in the YSR item pool and paralleling its discriminant profile on the PID-5.", 
"All displayed loadings were significant at p < .05.")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("ps > .05", "ps > .05"), Sentence = c("Daily Anankastia showed the strongest discriminant pattern overall-unrelated to PID-5 Negative Affectivity, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism (rs = .01-.08, all ps > .05)-though small significant correlations with PID-5 Antagonism (r = .23) and Detachment (r = .12) indicate the pattern was not entirely clean.", "Daily anankastia was essentially uncorrelated with every YSR scale (|r| ≤ .05, all ps > .05), consistent with the absence of Anankastia content in the YSR item pool and paralleling its discriminant profile on the PID-5." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed 114 self-reproducible output files (JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/Mplus) instead of R code.
-  114139 statistics stored from the extracted output.
-  21 of 53 reported tests matched (39.6%).
-  We found no R or Python code files to assess for reproducibility.

ethics_statements: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Bergische Universität Wuppertal (ref. no.
SK/AE 240113) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
live_data_statements: Participants were adolescents and young adults aged 14-21 residing in Germany who had migrated themselves or had at least one parent who had migrated; inclusion criteria were confirmed by telephone.
Most were still in school (69.68%), 20.32% were enrolled at university, and most described their financial situation as average (41.61%) or good (43.23%).
Consistent with a dimensional, transdiagnostic framework, participants were recruited to span a broad range of symptom expression, including adolescents engaged and not engaged in clinical services.
Participants completed an in-person debriefing session, with compensation following a tiered structure based on compliance (maximum €125) 1.

Participants completed on average 25.98 entries (SD = 4.54, Mdn = 28; 89.59% of possible, range = 13.79-100%); 95.48% of participants completed at least 50% and 82.26% at least 80% of surveys, meeting or exceeding typical compliance in adolescent daily-diary research on discrimination (60%-90%; Wang et al., 2026).
All participants, and a legal guardian of participants under 16, provided informed consent.

report: #### Mplus output (.out)

114 Mplus output files (`.out`) are present. A `.out` file always carries its own verbatim analysis syntax (under "INPUT INSTRUCTIONS"), so it is self-documenting. We extracted 7685 result tables (114139 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.
#### Reported vs. reproduced
53 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 21 matched (21 fully, 0 partially) — 39.6% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

text.text: Racial discrimination is a pervasive adolescent stressor, yet hierarchical-dimensional frameworks such as HiTOP have been validated in samples underrepresenting minoritized youth, and daily-level evidence on discrimination and youth mental health comes almost entirely from U.S. samples and narrow symptom sets.

In a preregistered 29-day daily-diary study of 310 ethnoracially minoritized adolescents (ages 14-21) in Germany (8,054 person-days), we evaluated a HiTOP-aligned daily symptom inventory and examined how daily racial discrimination and general stress related to symptom fluctuations.
Six factors replicated within persons, while the between-person structure resolved into three broader spectra.
Discrimination and general stress both predicted same-day symptom elevations; next-day associations were largely absent or indicated recovery.
Beyond general stress, discrimination showed incremental same-day elevations in internalizing, antagonism, disinhibition, and psychoticism, strongest for antagonism.
Discrimination operated as an acute, identity-relevant stressor not reducible to general daily stress.
Ethnic-racial discrimination is among the most consequential stressors adolescents face, yet it remains peripheral to theoretical models of how psychopathology emerges and unfolds in daily life.
Two limitations in the literature compound each other.

First, intensive longitudinal evidence linking daily discrimination to youth mental health comes almost exclusively from U.S. samples and narrow symptom sets, leaving open whether these dynamics generalize to other national contexts and to the broader space of psychopathology.

Second, the multidimensional frameworks increasingly used to map that space, most prominently the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP; Kotov et al., 2017 Kotov et al., , 2021)), have been validated predominantly in samples that underrepresent ethnoracially minoritized youth.

text.text: Instruments built on these taxonomies may therefore misread discrimination-related adaptations as psychopathology: vigilance toward threat, social withdrawal, and institutional mistrust can resemble symptom content that was never validated with this population in view (Rodriguez-Seijas et al., 2023).

text.text: The present study addresses both limitations with a 29-day daily-diary study of ethnoracially minoritized adolescents in Germany, examining how daily discrimination relates to withinperson fluctuations across a hierarchically organized set of symptom dimensions.
Adolescence is a period of heightened sensitivity to social stress, and discrimination is among its most pervasive forms (Benner et al., 2018; Cave et al., 2020).

text.text: Survey studies, largely from the United States, estimated that ethnoracially minoritized youth encounter discrimination once or twice a week in schools, public spaces, and institutional settings (Ortega-Williams et al., 2022; Steketee et al., 2021; Yip, 2018).

text.text: Cumulatively, these experiences were associated with elevated risk for depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress, and sleep disturbance, with compounding effects at intersecting marginalized identities (Polanco-Roman et al., 2024; Trent et al., 2019).

text.text: Germany offers an informative and understudied context: the proportion of schoolaged children of immigrant descent rose from 9.6% in 2005 to 39.1% in 2019 and forms a numerical majority in several metropolitan areas (Blossfeld et al., 2016; German Federal Statistical Office, 2021).

text.text: In this population, frequent discrimination in schools, public spaces, and police interactions has been documented, and perceived exclusion, that is, being denied recognition as "truly German," predicted depression, anxiety, and diminished institutional trust (DeZIM, 2025).

text.text: Daily-level evidence on discrimination and adolescent mental health in Germany is nonetheless essentially absent.
Addressing this gap requires treating discrimination experiences as conceptually distinct from general daily stress rather than as one entry in a broader inventory of adolescent stressors.

Whereas general stressors involve situational burden or challenge, discrimination carries an additional, group-based meaning, because the negative treatment is attributed to ethnic-racial group membership (Jones, 2000; Yip et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Whereas general stressors involve situational burden or challenge, discrimination carries an additional, group-based meaning, because the negative treatment is attributed to ethnic-racial group membership <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Jones, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Yip et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Two theoretical accounts explain why this attribution matters.
Social identity theory holds that group memberships form part of the selfconcept, so that threats to a valued group also threaten the self (Tajfel & Turner, 1979).
text.formatted: Social identity theory holds that group memberships form part of the selfconcept, so that threats to a valued group also threaten the self <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Tajfel & Turner, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: The rejection-identification model specifies that attributing negative treatment to prejudice signals rejection by the dominant group, with adverse consequences for well-being (Branscombe et al., 1999).
text.formatted: The rejection-identification model specifies that attributing negative treatment to prejudice signals rejection by the dominant group, with adverse consequences for well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Branscombe et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Discrimination experiences and general stressors may therefore both affect daily psychopathology, but only discrimination is theorized to carry identity-relevant threat.

According to stress process theory, chronic strains and acute daily stressors reinforce each other in shaping mental health: ongoing strain sensitizes individuals to everyday stressors, and recurrent daily stressors entrench chronic strain (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984; Pearlin, 1989).
text.formatted: According to stress process theory, chronic strains and acute daily stressors reinforce each other in shaping mental health: ongoing strain sensitizes individuals to everyday stressors, and recurrent daily stressors entrench chronic strain <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Lazarus & Folkman, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Pearlin, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Discrimination operates at both levels, as a chronic strain and as a recurrent daily stressor (Ong et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Discrimination operates at both levels, as a chronic strain and as a recurrent daily stressor <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Ong et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Because it targets salient social identities, it is not merely an external burden but a threat to self-worth and belonging, which may intensify this reciprocal escalation.

Capturing these dynamics requires designs that resolve experience at the timescale on which it occurs, in line with current views of psychopathology as a dynamic system of interacting symptoms and person-context processes (Fried, 2022; Hamaker & Wichers, 2017; Wright et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Capturing these dynamics requires designs that resolve experience at the timescale on which it occurs, in line with current views of psychopathology as a dynamic system of interacting symptoms and person-context processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fried, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hamaker & Wichers, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Wright et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A recent systematic review (Civitillo & Jugert, 2024) and meta-analysis (Wang et al., 2026) found robust concurrent within-person associations between daily discrimination and youth mental health, chiefly internalizing symptoms and sleep problems, whereas evidence on next-day carryover was equivocal; all but one of the reviewed studies, however, were conducted in the United States.

text.text: The scarce non-U.S. evidence is consistent with such day-level dynamics but does not test them directly.

A German study of Arabic-and Turkish-heritage adolescents found that school-based discrimination predicted same-day declines in cognitive engagement and next-day declines in emotional engagement (Civitillo et al., 2024), and research with asylum-seeking youth documented about five discriminatory events per two-week period (Müller et al., 2021).

text.text: Neither study examined within-person associations between daily discrimination and youth psychopathology.

In parallel with the growth of intensive longitudinal designs, psychopathology research has converged on hierarchical, dimensional frameworks that organize symptoms into transdiagnostic spectra and address well-documented limitations of categorical nosologies (Kotov et al., 2017 (Kotov et al., , 2021)).

text.text: Such frameworks are particularly suited to discrimination research.

Among Black Americans and Black individuals of Caribbean descent, racial discrimination was more strongly related to broadband internalizing and externalizing spectra than to specific PREPRINT: DISCRIMINATION AND DAILY PSYCHOPATHOLOGY IN YOUTH 6 diagnoses (Rodriguez-Seijas et al., 2015), and social stress in adolescence predicted internalizing and externalizing domains rather than any specific disorder over a 20-year follow-up (Conway et al., 2018).

text.text: The sample, however, was 70% White, and the authors cautioned against generalizing across cultures or languages.
The second question is whether the structure holds for ethnoracially minoritized youth outside the United States.
Its stakes go beyond psychometrics, because chronic exposure to discrimination may change how symptoms are felt, displayed, and reported (Rodriguez-Seijas et al., 2023).

text.text: Elevated detachment may partly reflect withdrawal as a protective response to hostile environments, and suspiciousness may reflect warranted mistrust of institutions with documented histories of bias (Kingston et al., 2023; Whaley, 2001).

text.text: Treating such responses as straightforward indicators of pathology risks pathologizing adaptation, so it is essential to first establish whether a hierarchical daily measure functions coherently in this population.

Coherent functioning has three testable aspects: the daily items should reproduce the expected hierarchical organization of symptom domains within and between persons (structural validity), individuals' average daily scores should converge with established trait inventories of the same constructs (between-person convergent validity), and day-to-day fluctuations should track same-day affect and functioning in theoretically expected ways (within-person convergent validity).

Treating discrimination as a dynamic daily stressor rather than a static exposure requires a measurement model spanning multiple symptom domains at multiple levels of generality, and a design that resolves stressor and symptom at the daily timescale.
Such a design allows discrimination to be related to symptoms on the day it occurs and the day after, and to be distinguished from general daily stress.
We pursued two aims.

The first aim was to evaluate the psychometric properties of a daily-diary adaptation of the Wright et al. (2025) hierarchical symptom inventory in ethnoracially minoritized adolescents (ages 14-21) in Germany.
text.formatted: The first aim was to evaluate the psychometric properties of a daily-diary adaptation of the <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wright et al. (2025)</ref> hierarchical symptom inventory in ethnoracially minoritized adolescents (ages 14-21) in Germany.

text.text: Because these analyses evaluate a measurement model in a new population rather than test directional predictions, we framed them as exploratory research questions.
We first asked which hierarchical structure of psychopathology emerges within and between persons (RQ1.1).

Extending the five-domain inventory of Wright et al. (2025) by psychoticism items, we expected six domains-Internalizing, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, anankastia, and psychoticism-to vary meaningfully from day to day and to covary similarly at both levels.
text.formatted: Extending the five-domain inventory of <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wright et al. (2025)</ref> by psychoticism items, we expected six domains-Internalizing, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, anankastia, and psychoticism-to vary meaningfully from day to day and to covary similarly at both levels.

text.text: We then asked to what extent individuals' average daily psychopathology levels align with established baseline inventories (PID-5, YSR; RQ1.2), anticipating convergence, and to what extent within-person fluctuations in daily psychopathology covary with daily affect, well-being, and perceived emotion regulation efficacy (RQ1.3), expecting higher negative affect and lower regulation efficacy on days with elevated symptoms.

The second aim was to test preregistered, theory-derived hypotheses about how daily ethnic-racial discrimination-directly and vicariously experienced, modeled both dichotomously and by perceived severity-and general stressors relate to symptom fluctuations, and to isolate discrimination's contribution beyond general daily stress.

Concurrently, we hypothesized that youth report elevated psychopathology on days with direct or vicarious discrimination relative to days without (H1.1), on days with more severe discrimination experiences (H1.2), and on days with higher general stress (H1.3).

Over time, we hypothesized that discrimination (H2.1), discrimination severity (H2.2), and general stress (H2.3) on day t predict elevated psychopathology on day t + 1, controlling for day-t psychopathology.
At the between-person level, we hypothesized that youth with more frequent or more severe discrimination or general stress report higher average psychopathology (H3).

text.text: We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
The study involved no experimental manipulations.

The daily-diary protocol assessed a broader set of constructs than addressed here, and the complete data-collection design included a four-day diary extension and a 6-day ecological momentary assessment phase, neither of which is analyzed in the present manuscript; all collected measures are listed in the OSF codebook (https://osf.io/dqv8f/)..

text.text: Participants.
Participants were adolescents and young adults aged 14-21 residing in Germany who had migrated themselves or had at least one parent who had migrated; inclusion criteria were confirmed by telephone.

The sample comprised 310 participants (M = 17.49 years, SD = 1.80), of whom 178 (57.42%) identified as female, 126 (40.65%) as male, and 3 as nonbinary; 2 preferred not to answer and 1 reported another gender identity.
Most were still in school (69.68%), 20.32% were enrolled at university, and most described their financial situation as average (41.61%) or good (43.23%).

Most participants (73.55%, n = 228) were born in Germany to one or both migrant parents; the remainder had migrated themselves, predominantly from the Middle East or West Asia (13.87 %, n = 43, mostly Syria) or South-East Europe (8.71%, n = 27; e.g., Poland, Ukraine, Greece).
Participants' reports of parental countries of origin were grouped into regions.
The most frequently represented regions were South-East Europe (32.67%, n = 99), the Middle East and West Asia (32.34%, n = 98), and North Africa (16.17%, n = 49).
Percentages refer to 303 regional classifications, with participants potentially represented in more than one region due to differences in their parents' countries of origin.
Nearly half identified as Muslim (47.42%), 30.97% as Christian, and 13.23% as atheist or nonreligious, while the remainder indentified with other specific religious or spiritual groups.
Power Considerations.
Because the dataset was designed as a resource for multiple research questions, the sample size target prioritized estimation precision over conventional statistical power.

Following Schönbrodt and Perugini (2013), we targeted a minimum of N = 250 for stable correlation estimates (±.10 precision) and oversampled to N = 300 ethnoracially minoritized youth to account for attrition (the larger data collection, targeting N = 450, also included participants without migration history).
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Schönbrodt and Perugini (2013)</ref>, we targeted a minimum of N = 250 for stable correlation estimates (±.10 precision) and oversampled to N = 300 ethnoracially minoritized youth to account for attrition (the larger data collection, targeting N = 450, also included participants without migration history).

text.text: Recruitment.
Consistent with a dimensional, transdiagnostic framework, participants were recruited to span a broad range of symptom expression, including adolescents engaged and not engaged in clinical services.
Recruitment drew on community networks, online platforms, and flyers; of 104 organizations contacted, 57 collaborated, most commonly schools (n = 40) and local clubs and associations (n = 17).
Eligibility required attendance at in-person baseline and closing sessions.

To reduce topic-related self-selection, the study was advertised as an investigation of adolescents' everyday experiences; during informed consent, participants (and parents of minors) were fully informed about all study content, including questions about discrimination and migration history.
Procedure.

The study used an intensive longitudinal design comprising a baseline assessment and a 29-day daily-diary phase, preceded by a pilot test of feasibility, notification timing, usability, and response logging.

Interested adolescents completed an online screening survey (age, gender, migration history) and a follow-up call confirming eligibility, then attended an in-person baseline session where they completed sociodemographic and dispositional questionnaires at a computer station, and installed the m-Path app on their personal phones, generating an anonymous participant ID.
The diary phase began immediately after baseline and ran for 28 consecutive days, plus one optional baseline-evening survey (maximum 29 entries).

Each evening at 19:30, participants received a notification to complete a ~7-minute survey on daily discrimination, stressors, coping, and well-being; surveys remained open until 23:30, with one reminder after 60 minutes and sequential item completion required.
Weekly phone check-ins addressed technical issues, encouraged compliance, verified discrimination reports, and confirmed continued residence in Germany.
Participants completed an in-person debriefing session, with compensation following a tiered structure based on compliance (maximum €125) 1.
Minoritization status was operationalized via migration history, defined as having migrated to Germany oneself or having at least one parent who had migrated (Starker et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Minoritization status was operationalized via migration history, defined as having migrated to Germany oneself or having at least one parent who had migrated <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Starker et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Status was assessed by online screening and confirmed in a follow-up phone call, with the phone confirmation taking precedence over discrepant screening responses.
Grandparental migration alone did not qualify participants for inclusion.
